\(355 \div 6 = 59\) remainder \(1\), since \(6 \cdot 59 = 354\).

So the base 6 representation of 355 ends in **1**.

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 21st century, a movie that turns the creation of facebook into something far more interesting than a simple business origin story. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, it is fast, intelligent, and emotionally cold in a way that perfectly fits its subject. rather than celebrating innovation, it examines ambition, resentment, loneliness, and the cost of being brilliant but deeply disconnected from other people.

one of the film’s greatest strengths is its screenplay. sorkin’s dialogue is famously quick and precise, and here it feels almost musical. conversations overlap, arguments escalate rapidly, and every scene seems to move with purpose. the script does not waste time explaining things the audience can already infer; instead, it trusts viewers to keep up with the legal disputes, the shifting alliances, and the emotional undercurrents. this gives the film a rare sense of intelligence without ever feeling like homework.

jesse eisenberg gives a remarkable performance as mark zuckerberg. he plays him not as a cartoon villain or a misunderstood genius, but as a socially awkward, hyper-focused young man whose intelligence is inseparable from his insecurity. eisenberg captures the character’s speed of thought and emotional distance with precision. mark is often cruel, but the performance makes clear that his cruelty comes from a mix of defensiveness, envy, and a desperate need to matter. it is a fascinating portrayal because it never asks for easy sympathy, yet it remains deeply watchable.

andrew garfield is equally strong as eduardo saverin, the co-founder whose friendship with mark slowly collapses under the pressure of money and betrayal. garfield brings warmth and hurt to the role, making eduardo the film’s emotional anchor. his scenes are especially effective because he represents something mark cannot fully understand: loyalty. when that loyalty is broken, the film becomes not just about a company, but about the destruction of a friendship that might have been genuine.

armie hammer’s dual performance as the winklevoss twins is one of the film’s most memorable technical and acting achievements. the twins could have been a gimmick, but hammer gives them a polished, almost aristocratic arrogance that makes them feel like real antagonists. their scenes add a layer of class tension to the story, suggesting that facebook’s rise was also a collision between old privilege and new digital power.

fincher’s direction is controlled and elegant. he gives the film a cool, polished visual style that matches the emotional detachment of the characters. the cinematography, editing, and score all work together to create a sense of momentum and unease. even scenes of people talking in rooms feel tense, as if every exchange is a negotiation or a threat. the film’s pacing is especially impressive because it covers a lot of ground without ever feeling rushed or bloated.

trent reznor and atticus ross’s score deserves special praise. it is eerie, propulsive, and modern, helping define the film’s atmosphere. the music does not simply support the scenes; it shapes them, giving the story a restless energy that mirrors the ambition and instability at its core. combined with kirk baxter and angus wall’s editing, the score helps make the film feel both intimate and epic.

what makes the social network so effective is that it understands that power often grows out of personal weakness. the film is not really about technology, even though technology is its setting. it is about exclusion, status, and the desire to be recognized. facebook becomes a symbol of connection, but the people building it are increasingly isolated from one another. that irony gives the movie its emotional force. the more successful the platform becomes, the more broken its creators seem.

the film also benefits from its ambiguity. it does not tell the audience exactly what to think about mark zuckerberg. he is brilliant, petty, driven, and lonely, sometimes all at once. the movie resists the temptation to turn him into a simple monster or a tragic hero. instead, it presents him as a product of his environment and his own choices, which makes him more interesting than a cleaner, more moral version would have been.

if there is any weakness, it is that the film’s emotional distance may leave some viewers cold. because it is so focused on wit, structure, and tension, it does not offer much in the way of warmth or catharsis. but that is also part of its design. the lack of sentiment is not a flaw so much as a statement. this is a story about people who are building a new world while failing to maintain the human relationships in front of them.

overall, the social network is a brilliant film: smart, stylish, and surprisingly tragic. it captures a specific moment in modern history while also feeling timeless in its depiction of ambition and betrayal. it is one of those rare movies that is both highly entertaining and genuinely insightful, and it remains as sharp now as it was when it was released.

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 2010s, and it remains just as impressive years after its release. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, the movie turns the messy origin story of facebook into something that feels both intimate and epic. it is not just a film about a website or a business dispute; it is a story about ambition, loneliness, betrayal, status, and the strange way modern success can be built on personal damage.

one of the film’s greatest strengths is its screenplay. sorkin’s dialogue is fast, precise, and often funny in a dry, cutting way. conversations move like verbal chess matches, with characters constantly trying to outthink, outmaneuver, or humiliate one another. the script gives the movie a relentless energy, but it also leaves room for sadness and regret. beneath all the cleverness, there is a deep emotional emptiness running through the story, and that contrast is what makes the film so memorable.

jesse eisenberg gives a brilliant performance as mark zuckerberg. he plays mark as brilliant, defensive, socially awkward, and emotionally guarded, but never as a simple villain. eisenberg captures the character’s speed of thought and his inability or unwillingness to connect with people in a normal way. mark is often unpleasant, but the performance is so controlled and layered that he remains fascinating. you can see both his intelligence and his insecurity at the same time, which makes him feel human rather than symbolic.

andrew garfield is equally strong as eduardo saverin. he brings warmth, loyalty, and hurt to the role, making eduardo the emotional center of the film. his betrayal hits hard because garfield makes it clear how much he believed in the friendship and how deeply he wanted to be part of something meaningful. armie hammer, playing both winklevoss twins, is also excellent. the dual performance is technically impressive, but more importantly, it gives the twins a polished, entitled arrogance that fits the film’s tone perfectly.

fincher’s direction is precise and controlled, which suits the material beautifully. he treats the story with a cool, almost clinical style, but that distance only makes the emotional damage more visible. the pacing is excellent, and the film moves between timelines in a way that keeps the tension high while gradually revealing how the relationships fell apart. the visual style is dark, elegant, and restrained, with a muted color palette that gives the movie a cold, modern feel. even scenes in crowded rooms or loud parties feel isolated, as if the characters are always separated from one another.

trent reznor and atticus ross’s score is another major highlight. the music is eerie, propulsive, and slightly unsettling, giving the film a sense of momentum and unease. it helps turn what could have been a straightforward business drama into something more haunting. the soundtrack never overwhelms the story, but it adds a layer of tension that lingers throughout the film.

what makes the social network especially effective is that it understands how personal and impersonal success can be at the same time. the movie is full of people chasing recognition, money, and influence, but it never presents those goals as satisfying. instead, it shows how achievement can come at the cost of trust and friendship. mark’s rise is portrayed as both impressive and tragic, because the thing he builds seems to isolate him even as it makes him powerful.

the film also works because it avoids easy moralizing. it does not simply condemn mark or glorify the people around him. instead, it presents a world where everyone is ambitious, insecure, and willing to compromise in different ways. that complexity gives the movie real depth. even when characters behave badly, the film understands their motives well enough to make them feel believable.

if there is any weakness, it is that the film’s emotional detachment may keep some viewers at arm’s length. its coolness is part of its style, but it can also make the story feel more admired than felt. still, that is a minor issue compared with how much the movie accomplishes. it is intelligent without being sterile, dramatic without being melodramatic, and stylish without feeling empty.

overall, the social network is a superb film: smart, tense, beautifully acted, and remarkably rewatchable. it captures a specific moment in tech history, but its themes are much broader and more lasting. it is about the cost of ambition, the fragility of friendship, and the way power can be built on emotional wreckage. few films balance intellect and feeling as well as this one does, and that is why it has earned its reputation as a modern classic.

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 2010s, and it remains just as gripping today as it was when it first came out. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, the movie turns the messy origin story of facebook into something that feels both intimate and epic. it is technically a film about a website and a legal dispute, but emotionally it is about ambition, loneliness, betrayal, status, and the cost of being brilliant and difficult at the same time.

one of the film’s greatest strengths is its screenplay. sorkin’s dialogue is fast, precise, and often funny in a dry, cutting way. every conversation feels like a duel, with characters constantly trying to outthink, outmaneuver, or humiliate one another. the script never wastes time explaining things in a heavy-handed way. instead, it lets the tension build through argument, contradiction, and subtext. even scenes that are mostly people talking in rooms feel charged with momentum. that is a rare achievement, and it is a big reason the movie never feels static despite being so dialogue-driven.

jesse eisenberg gives a remarkable performance as mark zuckerberg. he plays mark as brilliant, socially awkward, defensive, and deeply insecure, but never as a simple caricature. eisenberg captures the character’s speed of thought and emotional distance in a way that makes him fascinating even when he is unpleasant. mark is not portrayed as a traditional villain or hero. he is someone who seems to crave recognition while also resenting the people around him. that contradiction gives the film much of its power. you may not like him, but you understand why he behaves the way he does, and that makes him more unsettling.

the supporting cast is equally strong. andrew garfield brings real emotional weight to eduardo saverin, whose loyalty and eventual betrayal form the film’s most painful thread. garfield makes eduardo sympathetic without making him weak. armie hammer, playing both winklevoss twins with digital assistance, is surprisingly effective as the polished, entitled harvard elite who believe they were robbed. his performance adds a layer of arrogance that fits the film’s themes perfectly. justin timberlake also stands out as sean parker, bringing charisma and danger to the role of the older, more worldly disruptor who helps push facebook into a new phase. he feels like someone who understands the game better than everyone else, and that makes him both magnetic and alarming.

fincher’s direction is controlled and elegant. he gives the film a cold, precise visual style that matches the emotional distance of the characters. the cinematography, editing, and production design all work together to create a world that feels sleek but not sterile. the movie moves with incredible confidence, shifting between timelines without losing clarity or tension. fincher knows exactly how to make a conversation feel like a confrontation and how to make a room feel like a battlefield. even the quieter scenes carry an undercurrent of threat or regret.

trent reznor and atticus ross’s score is another major asset. the music is moody, electronic, and restless, giving the film a sense of forward motion and unease. it helps transform what could have been a straightforward business drama into something more haunting and modern. the score does not overwhelm the film; instead, it deepens the atmosphere and reinforces the feeling that these characters are always racing toward something they do not fully understand.

what makes the social network especially impressive is that it works on multiple levels at once. on the surface, it is a story about the creation of a massively successful company. underneath that, it is about friendship breaking apart under pressure, about the desire to be seen, and about how power changes people. the film also captures a very specific cultural moment: the early days of social media, when the internet still felt like a place where the future was being invented in real time. watching it now, the movie feels almost prophetic, because it understands that the technology itself is less important than the human motives behind it.

if there is a criticism to make, it is that the film is so tightly focused on wit, speed, and conflict that it sometimes leaves emotional space only in brief flashes. some viewers may wish for a little more warmth or a deeper exploration of the broader consequences of facebook’s rise. but that narrowness is also part of the film’s design. it is not trying to be a comprehensive history of the company. it is trying to capture the emotional truth of a particular kind of ambition and the damage it can cause.

overall, the social network is a brilliant film: intelligent, stylish, and emotionally sharp. it combines top-tier writing, directing, acting, and music into something that feels both entertaining and unsettling. it is a movie about the birth of a digital empire, but it endures because it understands something timeless about human relationships: success can be intoxicating, but it can also leave people isolated, bitter, and alone. that is what makes the film so memorable.

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 21st century, a movie that turns the origin story of facebook into something far more interesting than a simple tech biography. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, it is a film about ambition, resentment, loneliness, status, and the way genius can be tangled up with cruelty. even if you know the broad outlines of the real-life story, the movie still feels tense, elegant, and emotionally bruising from start to finish.

one of the film’s greatest strengths is its screenplay. sorkin’s dialogue moves with incredible speed, but it never feels empty or showy for its own sake. every conversation is loaded with subtext, especially the scenes between mark zuckerberg and the people around him. mark is portrayed not as a simple villain or hero, but as someone brilliant, insecure, defensive, and deeply unable to connect with others in a healthy way. jesse eisenberg gives the character a restless, almost electric energy, making him both fascinating and difficult to like. his performance captures the contradiction at the center of the film: a person who creates a platform for connection while seeming profoundly disconnected himself.

the supporting cast is equally strong. andrew garfield brings real emotional weight to eduardo saverin, whose betrayal feels painful because garfield makes him so earnest and vulnerable. armie hammer, playing both winklevoss twins with the help of digital effects, delivers a performance that is polished, arrogant, and strangely sympathetic. justin timberlake is also excellent as sean parker, bringing charisma and danger to the role of the older, more worldly disruptor who helps push facebook into a new phase. each character feels distinct, and the film uses their conflicts to explore different kinds of ambition and loyalty.

fincher’s direction is precise and controlled, which suits the material perfectly. the film has a cold, sleek visual style that mirrors the world it depicts: elite campuses, dimly lit rooms, glowing computer screens, and conversations that feel like negotiations for power. the pacing is excellent, and the editing gives the story a propulsive rhythm. even though much of the film consists of people talking in rooms, it never feels static. fincher makes every scene feel like it matters, and he builds tension out of arguments, legal depositions, and shifting alliances.

trent reznor and atticus ross’s score deserves special praise. it gives the film a haunting, modern pulse that feels both mechanical and emotional. the music helps create the sense that this is not just a story about a website, but about a new era of social life and digital identity. the soundtrack is memorable without overwhelming the film, and it adds a layer of unease that lingers long after the credits.

what makes the social network especially effective is that it understands how personal and impersonal the story really is. on one level, it is about the creation of a massively successful company. on another, it is about rejection, envy, and the desire to matter. mark’s actions are often cruel, but the film never reduces him to a cartoon. instead, it suggests that his genius and his emotional immaturity are inseparable. that complexity is what gives the movie its power. it is not interested in easy moral lessons; it is interested in the cost of being first, being smart, and being unable to trust anyone.

the film is also remarkably rewatchable because of how densely written and carefully constructed it is. there are so many small details, verbal jabs, and shifts in power that the movie rewards attention. it is the kind of film where a second viewing can feel even richer than the first, because you start to notice how every scene is doing multiple things at once. it is a legal drama, a character study, a business story, and a tragedy about friendship all at the same time.

if there is any limitation, it is that the film’s emotional distance may keep some viewers from fully connecting with the characters. its coolness is part of its style, but it can also make the story feel more analytical than intimate. still, that distance seems intentional, and it fits the film’s themes. these are people who are always calculating, always performing, always trying to win.

overall, the social network is a brilliant film: intelligent, stylish, and emotionally resonant in a very modern way. it captures the birth of a cultural giant while also telling a timeless story about ambition and alienation. it is one of those rare movies that feels both of its moment and likely to endure for years to come.

When your part of Earth is tilted away from the Sun:
- the Sun’s light is weaker
- the days are shorter
- it feels colder

That is winter.

Spring and fall happen in between, when neither side is tilted very much toward or away from the Sun.

\[
|x||x-5|=3
\]

### Case 1: \(x \ge 5\)
Then \(|x|=x\) and \(|x-5|=x-5\), so
\[
x(x-5)=3 \Rightarrow x^2-5x-3=0
\]
\[
x=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{37}}{2}
\]
Only \(x=\frac{5+\sqrt{37}}{2}\ge 5\) works.

### Case 2: \(0 \le x \le 5\)
Then \(|x|=x\), \(|x-5|=5-x\), so
\[
x(5-x)=3 \Rightarrow x^2-5x+3=0
\]
\[
x=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{13}}{2}
\]
Both are in \([0,5]\).

### Case 3: \(x \le 0\)
Then \(|x|=-x\), \(|x-5|=5-x\), so
\[
(-x)(5-x)=3 \Rightarrow x^2-5x-3=0
\]
\[
x=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{37}}{2}
\]
Only \(x=\frac{5-\sqrt{37}}{2}\le 0\) works.

So the real solutions are:
\[
\frac{5-\sqrt{37}}{2},\quad \frac{5-\sqrt{13}}{2},\quad \frac{5+\sqrt{13}}{2},\quad \frac{5+\sqrt{37}}{2}
\]

Their sum is
\[
\left(\frac{5-\sqrt{37}}{2}+\frac{5+\sqrt{37}}{2}\right)+\left(\frac{5-\sqrt{13}}{2}+\frac{5+\sqrt{13}}{2}\right)=5+5=10

the social network is one of the sharpest and most compelling films of the 21st century, a movie that turns the origin story of facebook into something far more interesting than a simple tech biography. directed by david fincher and written by aaron sorkin, it is a film about ambition, resentment, status, loneliness, and the way genius can be tangled up with cruelty. even if you know the broad outlines of the real-life events, the movie still feels tense and alive because it is less concerned with factual completeness than with emotional truth.

one of the film’s greatest strengths is its screenplay. sorkin’s dialogue moves with extraordinary speed and precision, full of wit, verbal sparring, and sudden emotional cuts. conversations often feel like battles, with each character trying to gain the upper hand through intelligence and confidence. mark zuckerberg, played by jesse eisenberg, is written as someone who is brilliant, defensive, and deeply insecure, and eisenberg captures that combination beautifully. his performance is fast, brittle, and slightly detached, but never flat. he makes mark seem like a person who is always thinking several steps ahead while also being unable to connect with the people right in front of him.

the supporting cast is equally strong. andrew garfield gives eduardo saverin a painful mix of loyalty, pride, and betrayal, making him one of the film’s most sympathetic figures. armie hammer, in a dual role as the winklevoss twins, brings a polished arrogance that works perfectly for the characters’ privileged confidence. justin timberlake is also excellent as sean parker, playing him as charismatic, reckless, and dangerously persuasive. each character feels distinct, and the film uses them to explore different forms of ambition and self-image.

fincher’s direction is controlled and elegant. he gives the film a cold, precise visual style that matches the emotional distance of its characters. the cinematography, editing, and score all work together to create a sense of momentum and unease. there is very little wasted movement in the film; every scene feels carefully designed to reveal character or advance conflict. even scenes of people talking in rooms feel suspenseful, because fincher understands that power struggles can be as dramatic as any action sequence.

what makes the social network especially effective is that it never reduces its characters to simple heroes or villains. mark is clearly difficult, often selfish, and sometimes cruel, but the film also shows how his intelligence and alienation shape him. the others are not purely innocent either; they are driven by ego, envy, and the desire to be recognized. this complexity gives the movie real depth. it is not just about who invented what, but about what happens when friendship, business, and identity collide.

the film also works as a portrait of a particular cultural moment. it captures the early 2000s tech world with a sense of inevitability, as if the rise of facebook were both accidental and destined. beneath the specific story, though, the movie is about something timeless: the loneliness that can exist even in a world built on connection. that irony gives the film much of its power. the platform that promises social connection is born out of isolation, exclusion, and the desire to belong.

if there is any weakness, it is that the film’s emotional distance can sometimes make it feel colder than it needs to be. some viewers may wish for more warmth or a deeper sense of the human cost behind the events. but that coldness is also part of the film’s design, and it suits the story it is telling. the ending, with mark repeatedly refreshing a page in hopes of a response, is quietly devastating because it reduces all the ambition and conflict to a simple, lonely gesture.

overall, the social network is a brilliant film: intelligent, stylish, and emotionally resonant in a restrained way. it is one of those rare movies that feels both of its moment and larger than it, a story about the birth of a company that becomes a study of ambition, betrayal, and the need to be seen. it is highly rewatchable, endlessly quotable, and still feels relevant years later.
